newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma gives in under cabinet pressure.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma gives in under cabinet pressure.

text.p: Russia's communist-dominated parliament gave in on Thursday to strong pressure from the reformist government and tentatively approved a draft tax code sought by ministers.
A total of 294 deputies backed a preliminary resolution to approve the code in principle. Only 80 voted against.
Deputies will present amendments and then vote later in the day on the final text of the resolution, which contains several clauses designed to help the Duma save face.
Ministers say the new package, which aims to help business by simplifying the tax system, is vital to put shaky state finances in order.
They say the 1998 budget will be in jeopardy unless the Duma gives initial backing to the code before its summer recess and have applied a carrot-and-stick policy towards the deputies.

Earlier this week the cabinet offered the Duma a compromise, allowing deputies until September to present amendments once the code passes the first reading. The resolution passed by the Duma said the second reading of the bill should start on November 1.

At the same time First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who is in overall charge of reforms, hinted the Duma might regret not backing the government on what he called "the issue of issues" and said "We consider the Thursday vote to be decisive".

Both government and opposition have denied rumours of a secret deal under which the Communists would back the draft while ministers would stop mentioning the possiblity of President Boris Yeltsin dissolving the legislature.
The Thursday vote somewhat equalled the score in the stand-off between the cabinet and the deputies.
On Tuesday the Duma threw out a package of bills to reduce or scrap most Soviet-era welfare benefits, which the cabinet says have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia.
The cuts would mostly affect the poor and elderly -- the main electorate of the opposition.
On Wednesday, the Duma again stalled a government plan to cut spending in the 1997 budget, but the government has said that the cuts will go ahead irrespective of the vote.
Yeltsin, meeting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin who has returned from a three-week Black Sea holiday, did not offer any immediate reaction to the Duma vote.
But, according to Interfax news agency, Yeltsin said: "On the whole things are not bad", in a clear sign of continued satisfaction with the efforts by the revamped government.

Later on Thursday Yeltsin is also due to record a regular radio address to the nation and give an interview to journalists from Russia and the Group of Seven countries -- the United States, Japan, France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Canada.
He then leaves for a G7 summit in Denver, where he will press Russia's case for full membership of the grouping, underlining its economic progress since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
